vignette: James, a 39-year-old airline pilot of Oceania descent, sought help after a harrowing encounter with police that left him feeling profoundly shaken. The traumatic event occurred during one of his routine flights when he was forced to make an emergency landing due to engine failure. Upon landing, the chaos at the airport escalated when local law enforcement responded aggressively and, in James's recollection, unnecessarily violently. This experience has deeply impacted how he perceives certain triggers and how they elicit heightened threat responses. James described his memory of that day as vividly terrifying. "Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time," he recounted, emphasizing how real and intense those memories remain. The trauma was so extreme that it made the entire episode feel surreal, almost like a movie scene rather than something that actually happened to him. This memory quality feeds into his triggers, making any physical proximity or driving with others particularly distressing. James’s fear of being in close spaces has intensified since the incident. Any time he is in crowded places, such as at the airport or on the tarmac near other planes and people, he feels an overwhelming sense of dread. "When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening," he explained. This heightened threat perception creates a vicious cycle; the more he fears these situations, the worse his symptoms become. His startle response to ordinary sounds has also escalated significantly. Even common airport noises like announcements or machinery now cause him to jump and feel as if danger is imminent. "I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people," James noted with a sense of frustration. This heightened vigilance makes every environment seem potentially threatening, particularly when he encounters strangers approaching him. James’s occupation exacerbates these symptoms; his job requires him to be in constant proximity to others and navigate various delays. "Driving with people" is another trigger that has intensified since the incident. When he drives with colleagues or family members, he feels on edge, constantly anticipating something going wrong. The fear of being trapped or overwhelmed by unexpected events has led James to avoid these situations as much as possible. The memory of that day continues to be a potent trigger for his threat responses. "My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things," he stated, indicating how these intense memories continue to influence his current state. This vivid recall makes him hyperaware of any signs of danger, reinforcing his avoidance behaviors. James’s divorce also adds another layer of complexity to his situation. The stress and instability from this life change have made it even more challenging for him to manage his symptoms. He is certain that something bad will happen again and feels constantly on guard, which has strained his relationships with former colleagues who do not understand why he avoids flying with them. Despite these overwhelming fears, James’s desire to return to a sense of normalcy and control over his life drives him to seek help. "What frightened me most was the realization that I could no longer function as an airline pilot without feeling like everything around me is a threat," he explained. He hopes therapy can provide tools to manage these overwhelming feelings and restore some semblance of stability in his daily life. James’s current state reflects a complex interplay between his triggers, memories, and perceived threats. The trauma from that day continues to shape how he perceives the world around him, making ordinary situations feel dangerous and unpredictable. As James begins therapy, he is hopeful for finding ways to break this cycle and reclaim control over his life.
